In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HCV may have protective effect against mortality from HBV-related diseases.
HCV suppresses mortality through decreasing HBV DNA level, and this effect is more evident in liver-related mortality.
HBV and HCV viral loads are independently associated with all-cause mortality, but the effect of HVC viral load on mortality is partially mediated through HBV DNA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effect of HVC mediated through HBV DNA on all-cause mortality was protective and that of HCV on liver-related mortality was also protective, but the latter effect was not significant for non-liver-related mortality.
HBV and HCV viruses have a coordinated effect on mortality, and the protective mediation effect of HCV viral level on mortality is mainly due to the suppression of HBV viral replication.
HBV viral load is an important mediator of mortality from liver-related causes, and HCV viral load is a suppressor of HBV viral level and thus mortality from liver-related diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HCV viral load is inversely associated with HBV viral load, and the effect of HCB mediated through HBV DNA is inversely correlated with mortality.
the two viruses may interact in a way that HCV may suppress the effect of HBV on mortality, and this may be mediated by decreasing HBV viral level in the liver.
